screens.title: What is Sculpt Mode?
screens.narratorSegment: Sculpt Mode is a specialized Blender workspace optimized for freeform, organic modeling. Unlike precise polygonal modeling where you place vertices and edges explicitly, sculpting responds to brush strokes that push, pull, smooth, or pinch the surface, giving you an intuitive, tactile workflow similar to working with clay. In practice you switch from the Layout or Modeling workspace into Sculpting, which updates the toolbar with sculpting brushes and presents settings that control how those brushes affect the mesh. Sculpt Mode matters because it lets you quickly iterate shapes and silhouettes without manual topology editing. A concrete example: when designing a stylized creature head, sculpting lets you block broad skull volumes with wide brush strokes, then refine the cheek and brow planes with smaller brushes to create believable anatomy. One common misconception is that sculpting always requires a high-poly base mesh. With Dyntopo active you can start from a low-poly cube or sphere and let Blender add geometry only where the brush needs it. Key takeaway: sculpting prioritizes form and flow, then topology can be retopologized later for production use. How will you use sculpting to express your silhouette?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Sculpt Mode treats the mesh like clay, enabling expressive shaping with brushes rather than manual vertex-by-vertex edits.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is Sculpt Mode?
Core idea

Sculpt Mode gives you brushes that behave like clay tools. Use broad strokes to shape silhouette then refine planes and surface detail.

Analogy: Digital clay — push and pull mass rather than moving vertices.
When to use: character heads, creatures, rocks, and natural shapes where organic flow matters.
Misconception: You do not need a high-poly base if you use Dyntopo; start simple and let topology follow form.
Key Takeaway

Sculpt Mode prioritizes visual form and silhouette. Use it to iterate shape quickly before fixing topology for production.

Sculpting example: creature head
Start with a sphere. Use large Draw or Clay Strips to block the skull and jaw. Reduce brush size to carve cheek and brow planes. Smooth frequently to blend planes before adding fine detail.
Checklist: Getting started
  • Switch to Sculpting workspace.
  • Choose a brush and set an appropriate size.
  • Enable Dyntopo if you need adaptive topology.
  • Work large-to-small: silhouette → planes → fine detail.

screens.title: Dyntopo — Dynamic Topology
screens.narratorSegment: Dyntopo, short for Dynamic Topology, is a Sculpt Mode feature that changes mesh tessellation on the fly as you brush. When enabled, brush strokes will cause Blender to subdivide or simplify the local triangles so detail appears where it’s needed and not everywhere. This is useful because you can start with a low-poly base—like a cube or sphere—and build complex organic forms without relying on pre-subdivided meshes. An example: pulling out an arm from a torso with Dyntopo active will create new faces along the stretched area so the surface keeps clean geometry instead of distorting a sparse mesh. The most important control is Detail Size: larger values produce coarser triangles suitable for primary blocking; smaller values produce finer triangles for wrinkles and pores. A common beginner mistake is choosing a too-small detail size early, which produces an overly dense mesh and can slow performance. A practical workflow is to block with large detail, then progressively reduce the Detail Size as you add secondary and tertiary forms. Always watch your polycount and target the level of detail needed for the final use—game assets often require restraint.

keyIdea.title: Dyntopo insight
keyIdea.text: Dyntopo creates adaptive geometry where you sculpt so you can start with simple bases and add topology only where needed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Dyntopo
Dyntopo explained

Dyntopo dynamically adds or removes triangles while sculpting so geometry is created where brush strokes demand it. This removes the need to pre-subdivide a mesh.

Detail Size: governs triangle scale. Start coarse for blocking, reduce for fine work.
Performance: smaller detail increases polycount. Monitor the status bar to avoid slowdowns.
Misconception: Dyntopo will always create perfect topology; it creates useful geometry for sculpting but not production topology for deformation—retopologize when required.
Key Takeaway

Use Dyntopo to sculpt forms from simple bases, but scale detail consciously to balance visual quality and performance.

Quick Dyntopo checklist
  • Activate Dyntopo from the Sculpt header.
  • Set Detail Size for current stage: coarse → medium → fine.
  • Use larger brushes for silhouette, small brushes for detail.
  • Watch polycount in Blender’s status bar.
Concrete example
Start with a sphere. Enable Dyntopo and set Detail Size to around 10–15 for rough blocking. Pull volumes with Draw, then reduce Detail Size for cracks and fine surface variation.
Common mistake
Choosing a small Detail Size at the beginning creates dense meshes before primary structure is finished. Begin coarse and refine.

screens.title: Essential Brushes: Draw and Clay Strips
screens.narratorSegment: Draw and Clay Strips are primary additive brushes used for building volume. The Draw brush adds or raises surface volume like pushing clay outward. Holding the Control key inverts it and carves inward, which is useful for cutting in shapes or creating crevices. Clay Strips builds forms as layered, overlapping strokes that resemble applying strips of real clay; this creates natural texture and is excellent for muscles, rock ridges, or layered anatomical forms. A concrete workflow: use Draw with a large brush and coarse Dyntopo to block the silhouette, then switch to Clay Strips with a slightly smaller brush to begin forming ridges and muscle groups. Always alternate with Smooth to blend strip edges so the surface reads as intentional form rather than patchy strokes. A common misconception is that Clay Strips must be used at high strength; instead, lower strength and multiple overlapping passes yield more believable structure. The takeaway is to treat Draw for broad mass and Clay Strips for layered sculpting—both are essential for expressive organic modeling. Essential Brushes: Draw and Clay Strips means use draw for broad mass and clay strips for layered, natural-looking forms; invert with control and blend with smooth frequently.. In practical terms, how to build primary and secondary forms with additive brushes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Draw & Clay Strips
Draw brush

Adds volume. Use large size and coarse Dyntopo for blocking. Hold Control to invert and carve inward.

When to use: primary silhouette and large forms.
Tip: multiple low-strength passes give more control than a single high-strength stroke.
Clay Strips brush
Builds forms in overlapping strips. Great for muscle groups and rock layering. Lower strength and repeat passes for natural results.
Practical example
Block a torso with Draw. Then use Clay Strips to add rib cage and shoulder volume, smoothing edges between strips to blend planes.
Common mistake
Overusing strength in Clay Strips produces chunky, unreal forms. Build up slowly and smooth between passes.

screens.title: Smooth and Grab: Blending and Silhouette
screens.narratorSegment: Smooth and Grab are two complementary tools that help make sculpted forms read well. Smooth removes harsh transitions and lumps, producing soft, believable planes by averaging the surrounding surface. In Blender, Smooth is typically activated by holding Shift while using any brush; developers and artists use it frequently between building passes. A practical example: after layering Clay Strips for muscle, use Smooth to blend the edges so the muscles transition naturally rather than appearing pasted on. The Grab brush is different: it moves an area of the mesh like a puppet, allowing you to change proportions and silhouette without changing local detail. Use Grab for big adjustments — for example, lengthening a snout or widening a torso — to explore silhouette early. A misconception is that smoothing removes detail you want to keep; instead, Smooth should be used selectively to maintain strong planes while removing surface noise. The combined workflow is clear: use Grab for silhouette adjustments, additive brushes for form, and Smooth constantly to harmonize the surface. This produces readable, art-directable sculpts suitable for later optimization. Smooth and Grab: Blending and Silhouette means use grab to change silhouette and smooth to blend surfaces; together they maintain readable form while you add or remove detail.. In practical terms, how smoothing and grab reshaping produce believable surfaces and proportions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Smooth & Grab
Smooth brush

Blend uneven surfaces and soften harsh edges. Activated by holding Shift with any brush. Use often to keep surfaces believable.

When to smooth: after building forms, to remove lumps and to prepare for finer detail.
Tip: alternate smoothing and building passes to retain form while removing noise.
Grab brush
Reposition larger masses without re-sculpting detail. Useful for silhouette and proportion edits before committing to fine shapes.
Concrete scenario
If a head reads too narrow, use Grab to widen the cheek area, then use Draw and Clay Strips to add volume, finishing with Smooth to blend edges.
Common mistake
Over-smoothing erases form. Smooth at moderate strength and keep an eye on major planes and silhouette.

screens.title: Progressive Refinement Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Progressive refinement is a disciplined workflow that keeps your sculpt readable and efficient. Start with primary forms: use a large brush, coarse Dyntopo detail, and broad strokes to establish silhouette and mass. The goal at this stage is proportion and overall volume rather than surface detail. Next, move to secondary forms: reduce brush size and Dyntopo detail to carve planes like cheekbones, brow ridges, and large muscle groups. This stage builds structure and gives visual cues for light and shadow. Finally, add tertiary details such as wrinkles, pores, and surface texture using very small brushes and finer detail settings. A practical example is sculpting a rock: block the overall mound, add large cracks and chips in the secondary stage, and finish with small nicks and surface granularities as tertiary detail. A common misconception is rushing to tertiary details before the structure is clear; this yields busy, unconvincing results. Key takeaway: discipline in stage progression preserves clarity and allows you to manage mesh density intentionally for game-ready assets. In practical terms, from primary blocking to tertiary detail. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Progressive Refinement
Step 1 — Primary
Large brushes, coarse Dyntopo, build silhouette and mass. Aim for correct proportion and overall readability.
Step 2 — Secondary
Smaller brushes and reduced Detail Size to carve planes, muscles, and major surface breaks.
Step 3 — Tertiary
Fine brushes for pores, small cracks, and texture. Only add this after structure is solid.
Example: sculpting a rock formation
Primary: large, irregular silhouette. Secondary: major cracks and protrusions with Clay Strips. Tertiary: small chips and grain with small Detail Size. Keep smoothing between stages to merge strokes naturally.
Avoid: tertiary detail too early.
Do: test silhouette at distance frequently.
Key Takeaway

Stage your work: blocking, structure, then detail. This keeps your sculpt readable and manageable.

screens.title: Mesh Density and Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Mesh density refers to how many triangles make up your sculpt and it affects both interactive performance and the cost of using the mesh in a game. Dyntopo makes density grow where you add detail, which is powerful but can unintentionally produce extremely dense regions if the detail size is too small. A clear example: carving many fine cracks at early stages with a tiny detail size may triple your triangle count and slow viewport performance. To balance quality and performance, adopt these practices: start coarse and only decrease Detail Size when you intentionally need tertiary detail; monitor the polycount in Blender’s status bar; and watch the silhouette at normal viewing distance — if shapes read well at that distance, you might not need extra micro-detail. In game asset workflows, consider baking detail into normal maps rather than overshooting mesh density. A common misconception is that more triangles always equal better quality; instead, efficient use of Dyntopo plus baking often yields the best visual result with acceptable performance. The takeaway is purposeful density management — detail where it matters, economize where it does not.

keyIdea.title: Density balance
keyIdea.text: Adaptive topology is useful but must be controlled. Monitor polycount and decide when geometry or normal maps are the right solution for final detail.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Mesh Density
Why density matters

High triangle counts slow viewport responsiveness and increase runtime cost in games. Dyntopo can generate dense geometry quickly if uncontrolled.

Practical rule: larger Dyntopo detail for blocking; progressively reduce for targeted fine work.
Measure: use Blender’s status bar to track polycount and pause to simplify if counts spike.
Key Takeaway

Balance local detail with overall performance. Bake micro-detail into textures when mesh density is not feasible.

Comparison
Dense mesh: true vertex detail but costlier. Normal map: cheaper at runtime but needs clean topology for baking.
Concrete tip
If polycount spikes, increase Dyntopo Detail Size slightly and smooth the area to reduce subdivisions, then continue refining selectively.
Misconception
More triangles do not always mean better visual fidelity. Strategic detail placement matters more than uniform density.

screens.title: Hands-on: Sculpting a Simple Rock (Step-by-step)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through sculpting a simple rock formation using the chapter's hands-on steps. Begin by opening Blender and switching to the Sculpting workspace. Delete the default cube and add a UV Sphere. Enter Sculpt Mode and activate Dyntopo from the viewport header. For the initial block, set Detail Size to a coarser value — around 10 to 15 in relative pixels — and use the Draw or Clay Strips brush to push and pull the sphere into an irregular mound. Frequently hold Shift and apply Smooth to remove sharp, unnatural transitions as you shape. Use the Grab brush to pull larger protrusions or push in depressions to create an interesting silhouette. screens.title: Brush Settings and Modifiers (Ctrl, Shift)
screens.narratorSegment: Brush settings and keyboard modifiers change how sculpting tools behave and can dramatically speed your workflow. Two modifiers are essential: holding Control inverts most brushes, turning additive actions into subtractive ones, which is invaluable for carving veins or creases without switching tools. Holding Shift temporarily switches to Smooth, letting you blend edges on the fly while working with any brush. Beyond modifiers, brush settings such as Strength and Radius determine how much a stroke affects the surface and how large the affected area is. Strength is best used with moderate values and multiple passes for control. Radius is often set relative to your current stage—large for silhouette, small for fine detail. A practical example: with Draw selected, reduce Strength and gently layer strokes rather than using full strength once; hold Control briefly to carve a groove, then hold Shift to smooth it back subtly. A common misconception is that higher Strength saves time; it usually sacrifices control. The takeaway: learn modifiers and settings as muscle memory to sculpt faster and with higher fidelity. screens.title: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Beginners commonly encounter a few recurring issues when learning sculpting. One is over-detailing too early: choosing a small Dyntopo detail size at the start creates a dense mesh without a defined structure. Fix this by stepping back to a coarser detail, smoothing, and re-blocking primary forms. Another pitfall is neglecting Smooth; many beginners leave visible lumps by not blending strokes often. The solution is to hold Shift regularly and make smoothing part of each pass. A third issue is working without checking silhouette: details that look impressive up close may ruin overall readability. Test your sculpt at distance and in silhouette to ensure major masses read clearly. Performance problems often result from uncontrolled Dyntopo growth; manage this by increasing Detail Size where fine detail is unnecessary and using normal maps later for micro-detail. Finally, avoid assuming sculpting produces production topology; retopologize when you need clean, deformable meshes. These fixes form a compact troubleshooting checklist that keeps your sculpts efficient and visually convincing. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome — in this chapter you will learn how Blender’s Sculpt Mode lets you shape organic, natural forms with an artist’s intuition. Sculpting treats your mesh like digital clay: brushes add or remove volume, smooth transitions, and move masses to build believable silhouettes. A key enabler is Dyntopo, or Dynamic Topology, which adaptively tessellates the mesh while you paint details so you can start with a simple base and let Blender create geometry where it’s required. You’ll also learn fundamental brushes — Draw and Clay Strips for building volume, Smooth for blending, and Grab for big silhouette changes — and the practical workflow of progressive refinement: block primary forms, define secondary planes, and reserve fine pores and wrinkles until the end. Throughout, we emphasize mesh density management and common beginner mistakes like over-detailing too early. By the end you’ll be ready to sculpt a simple rock formation that balances visual interest with efficient geometry suitable for game assets. Think of this chapter as the bridge from geometric modeling to expressive, organic creation. What will you build first?

In this chapter you will develop practical skills for sculpting in Blender. First, you’ll be able to confidently navigate the Sculpting workspace and understand the tools and panels that affect brush behavior and topology. For example, locating the Dyntopo toggle in the viewport header and identifying brush settings helps you control how geometry is created. Second, you will learn to use essential brushes — Draw, Clay Strips, Smooth, and Grab — and know when to build volume, blend surfaces, or reshape silhouettes. You’ll practice using Draw to add mass, Clay Strips for layered forms, Smooth to remove lumps, and Grab for large proportion adjustments. These skills matter because they let you translate artistic intent into efficient meshes. Finally, you’ll perform a guided hands-on sculpt of a simple rock formation to apply Dyntopo and brush selection while monitoring mesh density. This guided practice reinforces the workflow from primary blocking to fine detail so you can create game-friendly organic forms with confidence.

These additional objectives focus on practical application and avoiding common mistakes. You will learn to recognize and avoid early over-detailing, a frequent problem when sculptors choose a too-small Dyntopo detail size at the start. Instead, you will practice beginning with larger detail and progressively reducing it, maintaining a manageable polycount. You will also develop strategies to monitor mesh density, using Blender's status bar and by periodically judging silhouette and surface detail rather than raw polygon count. Another clear objective is to apply basic sculpting techniques to create initial organic shapes suitable for games: practicing blocking for silhouette, using Clay Strips for muscle-like forms, then smoothing transitions to avoid lumpy results. Finally, you will follow a hands-on activity sculpting a simple rock formation to connect settings, brush selection, and progressive refinement in a single, repeatable workflow. Each ability builds toward producing efficient, readable sculpts that balance artistic intent with game performance.

Sculpt Mode is a specialized Blender workspace optimized for freeform, organic modeling. Unlike precise polygonal modeling where you place vertices and edges explicitly, sculpting responds to brush strokes that push, pull, smooth, or pinch the surface, giving you an intuitive, tactile workflow similar to working with clay. In practice you switch from the Layout or Modeling workspace into Sculpting, which updates the toolbar with sculpting brushes and presents settings that control how those brushes affect the mesh. Sculpt Mode matters because it lets you quickly iterate shapes and silhouettes without manual topology editing. A concrete example: when designing a stylized creature head, sculpting lets you block broad skull volumes with wide brush strokes, then refine the cheek and brow planes with smaller brushes to create believable anatomy. One common misconception is that sculpting always requires a high-poly base mesh. With Dyntopo active you can start from a low-poly cube or sphere and let Blender add geometry only where the brush needs it. Key takeaway: sculpting prioritizes form and flow, then topology can be retopologized later for production use. How will you use sculpting to express your silhouette?

Dyntopo, short for Dynamic Topology, is a Sculpt Mode feature that changes mesh tessellation on the fly as you brush. When enabled, brush strokes will cause Blender to subdivide or simplify the local triangles so detail appears where it’s needed and not everywhere. This is useful because you can start with a low-poly base—like a cube or sphere—and build complex organic forms without relying on pre-subdivided meshes. An example: pulling out an arm from a torso with Dyntopo active will create new faces along the stretched area so the surface keeps clean geometry instead of distorting a sparse mesh. The most important control is Detail Size: larger values produce coarser triangles suitable for primary blocking; smaller values produce finer triangles for wrinkles and pores. A common beginner mistake is choosing a too-small detail size early, which produces an overly dense mesh and can slow performance. A practical workflow is to block with large detail, then progressively reduce the Detail Size as you add secondary and tertiary forms. Always watch your polycount and target the level of detail needed for the final use—game assets often require restraint.

Draw and Clay Strips are primary additive brushes used for building volume. The Draw brush adds or raises surface volume like pushing clay outward. Holding the Control key inverts it and carves inward, which is useful for cutting in shapes or creating crevices. Clay Strips builds forms as layered, overlapping strokes that resemble applying strips of real clay; this creates natural texture and is excellent for muscles, rock ridges, or layered anatomical forms. A concrete workflow: use Draw with a large brush and coarse Dyntopo to block the silhouette, then switch to Clay Strips with a slightly smaller brush to begin forming ridges and muscle groups. Always alternate with Smooth to blend strip edges so the surface reads as intentional form rather than patchy strokes. A common misconception is that Clay Strips must be used at high strength; instead, lower strength and multiple overlapping passes yield more believable structure. The takeaway is to treat Draw for broad mass and Clay Strips for layered sculpting—both are essential for expressive organic modeling. Smooth and Grab are two complementary tools that help make sculpted forms read well. Smooth removes harsh transitions and lumps, producing soft, believable planes by averaging the surrounding surface. In Blender, Smooth is typically activated by holding Shift while using any brush; developers and artists use it frequently between building passes. A practical example: after layering Clay Strips for muscle, use Smooth to blend the edges so the muscles transition naturally rather than appearing pasted on. The Grab brush is different: it moves an area of the mesh like a puppet, allowing you to change proportions and silhouette without changing local detail. Use Grab for big adjustments — for example, lengthening a snout or widening a torso — to explore silhouette early. Progressive refinement is a disciplined workflow that keeps your sculpt readable and efficient. Start with primary forms: use a large brush, coarse Dyntopo detail, and broad strokes to establish silhouette and mass. The goal at this stage is proportion and overall volume rather than surface detail. Next, move to secondary forms: reduce brush size and Dyntopo detail to carve planes like cheekbones, brow ridges, and large muscle groups. This stage builds structure and gives visual cues for light and shadow. Finally, add tertiary details such as wrinkles, pores, and surface texture using very small brushes and finer detail settings. A practical example is sculpting a rock: block the overall mound, add large cracks and chips in the secondary stage, and finish with small nicks and surface granularities as tertiary detail. Mesh density refers to how many triangles make up your sculpt and it affects both interactive performance and the cost of using the mesh in a game. Dyntopo makes density grow where you add detail, which is powerful but can unintentionally produce extremely dense regions if the detail size is too small. A clear example: carving many fine cracks at early stages with a tiny detail size may triple your triangle count and slow viewport performance. To balance quality and performance, adopt these practices: start coarse and only decrease Detail Size when you intentionally need tertiary detail; monitor the polycount in Blender’s status bar; and watch the silhouette at normal viewing distance — if shapes read well at that distance, you might not need extra micro-detail. In game asset workflows, consider baking detail into normal maps rather than overshooting mesh density. A common misconception is that more triangles always equal better quality; instead, efficient use of Dyntopo plus baking often yields the best visual result with acceptable performance. The takeaway is purposeful density management — detail where it matters, economize where it does not.

Two modifiers are essential: holding Control inverts most brushes, turning additive actions into subtractive ones, which is invaluable for carving veins or creases without switching tools. Holding Shift temporarily switches to Smooth, letting you blend edges on the fly while working with any brush. Beyond modifiers, brush settings such as Strength and Radius determine how much a stroke affects the surface and how large the affected area is. Strength is best used with moderate values and multiple passes for control. Radius is often set relative to your current stage—large for silhouette, small for fine detail. A practical example: with Draw selected, reduce Strength and gently layer strokes rather than using full strength once; hold Control briefly to carve a groove, then hold Shift to smooth it back subtly. A common misconception is that higher Strength saves time; it usually sacrifices control. The takeaway: learn modifiers and settings as muscle memory to sculpt faster and with higher fidelity. Beginners commonly encounter a few recurring issues when learning sculpting. One is over-detailing too early: choosing a small Dyntopo detail size at the start creates a dense mesh without a defined structure. Fix this by stepping back to a coarser detail, smoothing, and re-blocking primary forms. Another pitfall is neglecting Smooth; many beginners leave visible lumps by not blending strokes often. The solution is to hold Shift regularly and make smoothing part of each pass. A third issue is working without checking silhouette: details that look impressive up close may ruin overall readability. Test your sculpt at distance and in silhouette to ensure major masses read clearly. Performance problems often result from uncontrolled Dyntopo growth; manage this by increasing Detail Size where fine detail is unnecessary and using normal maps later for micro-detail. Finally, avoid assuming sculpting produces production topology; retopologize when you need clean, deformable meshes. These fixes form a compact troubleshooting checklist that keeps your sculpts efficient and visually convincing. Sculpting for games requires a balance between artistic detail and practical constraints. The sculpting stage focuses on silhouette and localized surface detail. Later you’ll often retopologize the result to create an optimized mesh suitable for animation and performance, or bake high-frequency surface detail into normal maps for use on a low-poly model. When sculpting for a game asset, target areas where topology must be dense — like deformation zones — and use Dyntopo selectively elsewhere. A concrete scenario: for a character's head, ensure clean edge flow around the mouth and eyes during retopology, while sculpting fine pores on the high-poly model and baking them into textures. A common misconception is that the sculpt must be final topology; instead, treat the sculpt as a source of visual information to be translated into production-friendly geometry and maps. These are the core ideas to carry forward. First, Sculpt Mode is an artistic, brush-driven workflow that treats meshes like digital clay and is ideal for organic shapes. Second, Dyntopo dynamically tessellates the mesh where brushes need detail, letting you start from simple bases and add geometry gradually — but control Detail Size to avoid unnecessary density. Third, brushes have distinct roles: Draw and Clay Strips build mass and layered forms, Smooth blends transitions, and Grab adjusts silhouette. Keep the progressive refinement workflow in mind — block primary forms, define secondary planes, then add tertiary detail. Finally, watch mesh density and plan for retopology or baking when producing game assets. These ideas help you sculpt effectively while keeping assets performant and production-ready.
